short: Native rule restored after the Mongols, and the China that Europe first met.
full:
A peasant rebel, Zhu Yuanzhang, drove the Yuan out and took the throne in 1368 as the Hongwu Emperor. His son the Yongle Emperor moved the capital from Nanjing to Beijing in 1421, built the Forbidden City there, and sent Zheng He's fleets across the Indian Ocean. Within a generation the court reversed course: the voyages stopped, private overseas trade was banned outright for long stretches, and the defensive effort went into the brick and stone wall lines still standing on the northern frontier.

The Ming were nonetheless deeply connected to the wider world. Silver from Spanish America and Japan flooded in through Manila and Macao in exchange for silk and porcelain, and taxes were consolidated into a single silver payment. Novels, drama and porcelain of the period define the Chinese decorative tradition. Falling silver imports, fiscal crisis, famine and army mutinies converged in the 1640s. The rebel Li Zicheng entered Beijing in April 1644 and the Chongzhen Emperor hanged himself on Coal Hill; Manchu forces took the capital weeks later.
